In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
Simulation results for a mobile robotic arm in 2D and 3D environments demonstrate the method's efficacy in achieving collision-free navigation while maintaining a stable trajectory.

Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators – sentence overlap and edit distance – are employed for gauging sentence similarity.

We introduce a novel quantum gate design suitable for bosonic systems, which overcomes limitations of existing linear gates. Our approach leverages unitary coupled-cluster states and nonlinear interactions in a Bose-Einstein condensate to execute the desired quantum operations. The proposed gate architecture exhibits greater resilience to errors and noise compared to linear gates, and we illustrate its effectiveness with a practical example of implementing the CNOT gate within a 2D BEC using a specific laser setup.

This paper aims to accomplish two distinct objectives. Firstly, it seeks to establish a unicity theorem for meromorphic mappings from a complete Kähler manifold to a complex projective space, under the constraint of limited intersection with hypersurfaces. Secondly, the paper aims to prove a unicity theorem for the case of nondegenerate meromorphic mappings that share a specified number of hyperplanes in a particular geometric configuration.

Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. Historically, the nondegenerate locus has been obtained using ideal-theoretic techniques like saturation ideals and equidimensional decompositions. We propose an algorithm leveraging signature-based features of Gröbner basis algorithms to efficiently calculate the nondegenerate locus of polynomial systems.

Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess in the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass distribution over hadronic contributions, we found that quasi-real direct virtual photons significantly contribute to the photon spectrum. In Cu$+$Cu collisions, photons show a clear increase above a binary-scaled $p$$+$$p$ fit, and their transverse momentum spectra follow a similar trend as Au$+$Au collisions, involving a similar number of participants. We have determined the inverse slopes of the photon $p_T$ distributions, which are comparable to those found in Au$+$Au collisions, and observed that the photon $p_T$ spectra can be described by a modified power-law model in the entire measured $p_T$ range.

The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We develop a new method for determining hypergraph extremality and apply it to calculate the asymptotic extremal function of the tetrahedron graph under our novel framework. The codegree squared sum, or co2(G), is introduced to measure codegree magnitude in a 3-uniform hypergraph, with exco2(n,H) representing the maximal codegree squared sum among n-vertex H-free hypergraphs. Utilizing flag algebra computations, we determine the codegree squared extremal numbers for K4^3 and K5^3 and demonstrate associated stability properties, revealing the structural resemblance of extremal K4^3-free hypergraphs to the conjectured extremal hypergraphs of Turan's tetrahedron problem. Additionally, we identify key general characteristics of exco2(n,H), such as the existence of a scaled limit and invariance under vertex blow-up.

Achieving a seamless visual experience in map line joins has long been challenging, particularly when dealing with anti-aliasing effects. The conventional approach to anti-aliasing involves employing vertex, pixel,, and multisample techniques but these require significant processing power. The implementation of modern graphics engines, including those on mobile devices, often relies on a limited subset of these methods. The limited capabilities of these engines result in distorted shapes and visible edges when using anti-aliasing techniques, hindering a smooth visual experience. A more efficient anti-aliasing method is needed to replace the standard techniques to provide a better user experience. The development of a new rendering pipeline, Spatial AA, addresses this need by improving the anti-aliasing efficiency. Spatial AA utilizes two key components: spatial indices and an aggregate kernel. The spatial indices component optimizes data processing by combining adjacent triangle blocks and reducing the number of operations, thereby minimizing memory consumption. The aggregate kernel leverages GPU capabilities to perform simultaneous rendering operations across multiple blocks. The implementation of Spatial AA eliminates the need for frequent index switching, a common issue in conventional anti-aliasing methods, to achieve a notable increase in rendering efficiency of up to 70%. Additionally, Spatial AA facilitates real-time rendering of complex maps that incorporate detailed cityscapes, forest areas, and mountain terrains with anti-aliasing effects at a rate of over 60 frames per second.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy.

Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas, as well as their escape from pulsar wind nebulae. Research on pulsar halos has brought to light that their associated diffusion coefficient is substantially lower than the overall average in the Galaxy, thus generating considerable interest among scientists. We delve into the recent breakthroughs in the study of pulsar halos, including the distinct properties of these sources, identified pulsar halos, theoretical mechanisms underlying their exceptionally slow diffusion, their pivotal roles in investigating cosmic-ray propagation and particle injection, and the implications for constraining the diffusion coefficient based on the pulsar halo's size. Moreover, the chapter concludes by discussing the potential for future research on pulsar halos.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or image analysis, have significant drawbacks due to limited coverage and reliance on existing infrastructure.
A major obstacle in using machine learning for weather detection is the lack of a reliable and comprehensive image classification dataset.
To address this issue, we have introduced the Weather4SLAM dataset, which contains high-quality images for seven distinct weather types and has been made publicly available for further research enhancements.
We have also developed a novel data augmentation technique centered on image filtering to enhance model performance and reduce training complexity.
A comprehensive evaluation of traditional Convolutional Neural Networks has been conducted, involving multiple experiments to identify the most effective approaches.

Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, scientists display a more steady interest pattern, as captured through web searches. Furthermore, we discover a significant link between scientists and the general public, as well as between economists and politicians, as we normalize the data for comparison purposes.

Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In response, researchers have turned to data-driven methods. However, current methods typically require extensive model learning through simulations or offline processes, which can be impractical or time-consuming. This limitation hampers real-time high-performance control applications. In response to this constraint, this paper introduces a novel online data-driven controller based on the Koopman operator theory. The proposed method learns and updates the controller in real-time, integrating online model learning, dynamics system reduction, and optimal control into a single, integrated approach. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this controller through successful grasping operations in complex environments using multi-fingered soft grippers.

One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the lowest cost value for a given function, known as an optimization problem. Various numerical methods have been proposed to solve this problem, but the Gradient Descent method remains the most popular due to its ease and effectiveness. Nonetheless, this approach faces challenges with local minima and slow convergence, particularly when near the optimal point. To address these issues, the Natural Gradient Descent method was developed, leveraging specific properties of the cost function and its gradient to enhance performance. This work demonstrates that NGD relies on underlying symmetries, constraining them to only work with cost functions with consistent scales and orientations. Despite these limitations, NGD still outperforms GD in many scenarios, according to our numerical tests.

High-energy emissions from ancient supermassive black holes can provide a direct look into the black hole activity in the early universe. Specifically, misaligned jets of high-redshift active galaxies should make up a significant portion of these distant galaxy populations. This study uses a highly detailed analysis of data collected from multiple observations of a particularly old and distant galaxy called J2102+6015. High-definition images of this galaxy were taken through multiple phases of activity in 2017 and 2019, and a highly complex pattern of energy emission was detected during the latter period. Analysis of the images indicates that this galaxy is significantly older than initially thought and exhibits characteristics consistent with an evolving, youthful jet activity pattern. Given that this galaxy is only about 1 billion years old, it presents a valuable tool for studying jet evolution and can potentially provide vital insights into the underlying physics driving these patterns in the early universe.

This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite years of effort from oncologists, remains imperfect. Current models, whether based on cancer characteristics or patient health, can't accurately predict survival times for every patient. We introduce a novel approach that combines cancer-related image and text data to identify factors affecting survival. Our model, driven by long short-term memory cells, is specifically designed to process the complex, multi-faceted data inherent in lung cancer. By incorporating a text representation module, we've significantly enhanced our model's performance and gained deeper insight into how different data types interact. Results show that our method surpasses existing single-modality models and provides more accurate predictions than models based on fewer data types. Additionally, it enables us to determine the relative importance of each data type and how they intersect, ultimately providing a foundation for more comprehensive research.

A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies.

A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra analysis. By leveraging sophisticated simulations of cosmic structure formation, a substantial dataset of absorption spectra and associated density perturbation maps are generated. With these maps, a neural network is trained that can predict the density power spectrum from the spectra, achieving reconstruction accuracy of 10% for wavelengths longer than 1000 comets and 10% error in mass density at z=3.5. This method enhances the future quasar spectroscopy projects such as the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument and MOONS by utilizing the existing or soon-to-be-collected quasar spectra to map the cosmic structure and aid in systematic bias analysis.

This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type. Initially, we establish the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to $U(\frak h)$ are one-dimensional. Next, we identify the requirements for the Lie algebra of a parabolic type to have a module that is $U(\frak h)$-free, specifically free as a $U(\frak h)$-module. We then generalize these findings to cover Lie algebras of the Weyl type, focusing particularly on irreducible modules in the context of infinite rank.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this progress, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge,
primarily due to the need for extensive data alignment between the model's training
and operational datasets. To overcome this limitation, our proposed framework
envisions a two-phase architecture that allows for pre-training on vast language
models and subsequent fine-tuning on user-defined dialogue requirements.
Furthermore, our framework is designed to be dynamically adaptable to shifting
user preferences without necessitating system revisions. Through thorough
experiments and user evaluations, our system successfully achieves role-specified
open-domain conversations by leveraging large-language models, thereby addressing
the data alignment issue and showcasing its potential for real-world applications.

The 2015 detection of GW150914, the most powerful gravitational wave event observed so far, marked a pivotal moment in science, opening doors to new areas of research. Notably, it enabled direct measurement of a novel phenomenon - gravitational wave memory. We investigate the stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) resulting from unresolved events creating gravitational wave memory. To do so, we employed a mathematical framework for describing gravitational wave memory radiation. Our analysis produces an expression for the SGWB intensity, tied to the event rate and gravitational wave characteristics. Ultimately, we find that the SGWB caused by gravitational wave memory could be non-negligible, potentially exceeding that generated by binary black hole mergers in certain scenarios.

A hypothetical supersymmetry framework offers an explanation for why large particles weren't discovered by the Large Hadron Collider; this framework predicts the universe went through a phase transition around the time of the universe's birth that may create ripples in space time that scientists could detect. Developing a realistic model based on how this supersymmetry is broken, researchers found this phase transition can lead to masses in certain heavy particles that may create more particles and a new theory of neutrino mass, as well as ripples in space time that may signal the universe's birth. The same model can help predict signs of these early ripples in space time that may signal the universe's birth. The universe's phase transition can potentially create tiny, extremely dense regions known as black holes that date back to the universe's birth.

A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity in the future. A novel approach to this challenge is presented, incorporating an emergent signaling game framework with a neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence system that facilitates causal reasoning. To design a context-specific communication language, an alternating maximization algorithm optimizes utility values between communication nodes. This language enhances the vocabulary of semantic communication to encompass complex data descriptions, and simulates data transfer to evaluate the proposed system's performance in specific scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework, as it achieves better results than conventional methods, and showcase the potential for seamless and efficient data transfer in semantic communication networks.

The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods in the past. However, individually, these approaches often fail to yield practical results in real-world applications. To address this limitation, a new word prediction model is proposed, which integrates the Naive Bayes and Latent Information methods in this paper. By fusing these two techniques, the hybrid model leverages the benefits of both, enhancing accuracy and providing a semantic word context for better results. Furthermore, a dataset of Latvian language word pairs, LIWP, has been created to support model testing and evaluation. The hybrid model demonstrates superior performance, outshining existing models based on semantic analysis.

Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with high recall rates compared to conventional methods. Recent techniques have primarily focused on modeling item co-occurrence statistics from publicly available datasets. However, these models overlook the underlying ranking information of items within actual user sessions, which is a crucial aspect for effectively discovering new items. This research proposes a novel framework consisting of two stages for enhancing item discovery and recommendation performance. Firstly, a rank-aware item embedding network is trained to capture nuanced item representations based on their occurrences across user sessions. Secondly, a light-weight recommender model is applied to generate personalized suggestions by leveraging the trained item embeddings. Experimental results on diverse public datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over existing benchmark models.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties simultaneously, leading to stable placement at sites with moderate activity levels. We validate our analytical findings through detailed simulations. This study offers insights into how single active cells respond to activity gradients by facilitating the exploration of new locations or the retention of preferred environments.

A thorough approach is outlined to simulate single-phase flow in fractured porous media. The proposed method involves three main components: fracture mapping, mesh generation, and solution processing. The mesh generation stage is particularly critical as it directly affects the accuracy of the solution. Two distinct methods are employed to build the fracture matrix model: a surface mesh construction method and an enclosed mesh construction method. Both methods utilize a multi-dimensional meshing approach to create the fracture pore space. Once the fracture matrix model mesh is obtained, a conventional finite difference or finite element method can be used to solve the flow equations. Alternatively, a more versatile mimetic finite difference method is introduced to solve the fracture matrix model. The proposed method is thoroughly demonstrated with two-dimensional and three-dimensional case studies.

This study centers on the development of techniques to maintain, recreate, and steer formations of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). A novel algorithm using the Iterative Closest Point method, tailored for real-time implementation on autonomous systems, is introduced to reassemble UAV formations quickly. Furthermore, a simple collision avoidance system is incorporated, drawing from potential field methods and integrating with the ICPICP algorithm to test its efficacy in dynamic environments. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of these tools and offer potential applications for this research include aerial photography and surveillance operations.

This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the minimum number of unique eigenvalues, eigenvalue limits, the characteristic polynomial, and bounds for the Seidel energy of a chain graph, which outperform previously proposed energy bounds by Haemers. We also obtain the minimum Seidel energy for specific chain graphs of order $n$, along with presenting several unresolved questions.

In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the SDDE's delayed fractional Brownian component, the current dies down slowly and isn't ergodic, which differs from standard stochastic processes. We make use of the fractional White Noise calculus and establish key existence, uniqueness, and stability theorems necessary for formulating a suitable fractional Brownian motion. We then introduce a fundamental result stating that, under certain conditions, the solution to the delayed SDDE remains stable when compared to the solution of an associated differential equation that doesn't take into account the delay, thus establishing an link between the two. We demonstrate that these theoretical results can be applied to develop an essential mean-field optimal control issue for delayed SDDEs driven by fractional Brownian motion. Our study provides a means to translate the concept of maximum principle and necessary conditions of optimality, which is particularly relevant to applications involving delayed systems in finance and other fields.

We've developed a unique, detailed two-parameter set of finite-band Jacobi elliptic potentials that correspond to the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator, seamlessly linking two well-known limit cases, each associated with the absence or presence of elliptic parameters. To thoroughly analyze the Dirac operator's spectrum, we've made connections between periodic/antiperiodic eigenvalue problems for the operator, equivalent tridiagonal operator actions in weighted Hilbert spaces and relevant Heun equation connection issues. This, in turn, ties into four related non-self-adjoint, unbounded tridiagonal operator eigenvalue problems which surprisingly possess real eigenvalues.

RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with users; however, congestion areas are often poorly served due to high data traffic, weak signals, and interference, which can be addressed through the use of vehicle relays. To enhance the network in these situations, this research utilizes stochastic geometry to develop an innovative 2-tier heterogenous vehicular network model. By positioning RSUs as point-processes and equipping a few of them with vehicle relays, which serve as effective relays, this model aims to increase the coverage area and enhance data transfer speed. The analysis involves calculating the probabilities of user coverage, data transfer success, and interference levels, which are then validated through simulations. The results indicate that the incorporation of vehicle relays significantly boosts the network performance of RSUs in terms of coverage, success rates, and overall data transfer speed.

Wikipedia's reliability relies heavily on its editors, as they play a key role in ensuring accuracy by identifying and fixing inaccuracies, verifying sources, and maintaining article quality. However, articles requiring the most attention often belong to lower quality pages that need improvement. While editors spend time enhancing high-quality articles, these lower quality pages often go unattended. In an effort to bridge this gap, our research focuses on developing an innovative method that employs machine learning to label articles that require the most editorial assistance, with positive results.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the internal network parameters, which isn't always possible due to model complexity or data protection constraints. A new approach tackles this issue by developing a method that can leverage the output of a black-box black-box model, describing its behavior as the result of a series of decisions rather than feature mappings. As a result, this approach can train a distillation model without requiring access to the complex model's code, making it suitable for a wider range of applications.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from LHCb, theoretical predictions, PDG data, and possible resonance contributions respectively.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$ action, we establish a simple method for achieving this transformation. Our work rigorously formalizes concepts seen in string theory applications and addresses a variety of background-dependent issues, such as the choice of Molimor-Morita equivalence. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the Molimor-Morita braid group action resulting from the T-dual of a torus bundle.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework. This novel approach leverages peer agents' successful experiences through multi-agent reinforcement learning to train imitation models, eliminating the need for expert input. We have theoretically proven the connection between our method and maximum likelihood imitation learning and supported this with experimental results from various domains, including Atari games and a complex robotic task.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, the average computation of our metric outperforms previous alternatives by 57%. By reducing computations, the overall efficiency of our method surpasses existing approaches, achieving a 2.5 times improvement.

This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud-based hand joint tracking system, to calculate hand joint movement between frames. Our novel hand pose canonicalization method allows for tracking of deformed hand images, and a temperature-based clustering technique matches hand joints across frames. Additionally, we leverage a prior shape model to refine our hand-only reconstruction approach. Our method is the first to provide accurate hand and object tracking in a sequence of point clouds, and we validate its effectiveness through comprehensive experiments on a large and diverse real-world dataset called ManoNet, consisting of over 300K hand samples. Our code and dataset will be open-sourced.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram when reduced modulo 3, resulting in a generated complex reflection group. We demonstrate that this reduced group exhibits Artin symmetry and possess a real representation, in addition to an equivalent permutation group based on 8 elements.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector in a robot-assisted depth video frame. A straightforward hand-coding system is also implemented to convert these models into a suitable robot coordinate system. Through analysis, our method's dependence on object recognition and object pose estimation is minimized, thereby enhancing its robustness and general applicability. Our research demonstrates that deep learning can effectively address complex industrial tasks and overcome limitations in dynamic environments.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units connected through complex networks, with an emphasis on defining the concept's mathematical representation and developing a framework to detect its presence. This framework achieves two key objectives: it provides a direct method to establish the interdependence of units and identifies the specific paths through which treatment interference occurs. Both of these tasks were previously considered high-ranking challenges in the field. By modeling treatment interference, insights can be gained on its impact and potential ways to address it, with applications in settings where treatment non-equivalence changes over time. Illustrating the utility of the proposed framework are two real-world scenarios: analyzing the extended effects of a pandemic and the spread of information within a social network.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a star are being conducted. In the core of a star that has not yet undergone nuclear reactions, it's observed that the interactions between these particles and the star's constituent atoms via a particular particle can produce an unusually high number of neutrinos, which may equal or surpass those produced by supernovae explosions. This process primarily involves two reactions: a collision of two dark matter particles resulting in neutrinos or intermediate particles that then decay into neutrinos, which may be confined to less than 1-2 percent of the star's mass. This process can potentially heat a star and may impact the cooling curves of a star over time. This process can potentially heat a star and may impact the cooling curves of a star over time.

The ongoing CFIS survey on the Canadian Forking Intermediate Large (FIDL) telescope, which crosses the Canada-US border, has made public their data in the red, i-filter, and g' bands. After conducting a thorough photometric analysis for the survey's magnitude-limited data set, we employed the ShapePipe pipeline to measure the complex elliptical morphology of roughly 6 million well-detected galaxies within a 412 square-degree area. Compared to other popular pipelines, ShapePipe distinctively incorporates a unique method for modeling complex elliptical galaxies and utilizes adaptive sparse convolution for quicker computation. For the studied region, we reported our findings on galaxy elliptical orientation, overall density patterns, and correlated structures. Additionally, we used the measured shapes to examine the relationship between galaxy surface brightness profiles and their sizes. Ultimately, we used the shapes to create a reliable map of large-scale cosmic distortion for the UNIONS/CFIS area.

A notable consequence of a finding by J. S. Wang and Q. Zhang has been the creation of a novel Li-Yau type estimate, which has also given rise to a new perspective on the second Lyapunov constant. This constant's behavior can be likened to that of a transitive measure under the action of a certain group of matrices. Building upon the work of J. S. Wang and Q. Zhang, as well as C. McMullen, researchers have established a new set of estimates regarding the distribution of certain matrices, which has also led to the discovery of unique patterns in both the Farey sequence and the set of rational numbers, as well as insights regarding the location of diagonal irrational numbers within these sets. Notably, the obtained results can be applied to a wide range of n-dimensional environments.

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2]. As an additional finding, for quasi-exceptional pairs (X, D) where D is a divisor on X, standard k-rationality of X applies if and only if the pair (X, D) is k-rational. This concept of k-rationality for pairs extends existing theories and may have potential uses in studying singularities, as it adheres to established rules regarding local vanishing phenomena.

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a linear chain of ferric wheels, where the magnetic properties shift from an antiferromagnetic state to a ferromagnetic state. Utilizing nuclear magnetic resonance techniques to measure the transverse spin correlations in real-time, we've tracked the dynamics of spin fluctuations on both local and distant levels. Our research indicates that the intermediate stages of the magnetic transition exhibit BKT characteristics, where the correlation length grows rapidly in an exponentially field-dependent manner. This phenomenon aligns with theoretical predictions made by van den Brink and co-authors in 1998.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs mass. The model, referred to as $a
u$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis within the context of neutrino, axion, and sterile neutrino dark matter. Constraints are imposed by various data sources including neutrinoless double beta decay, axion emission from sun, kinetic mixing measurements, and dark matter probe through xenon nucleus. The analysis reveals the existence of sterile neutrino parameter space that accommodates dark matter distributions in agreement with data from simon et al. (SIMON2019) and also aligns with measurements from xenon1ton. within the context of neutrino properties. Additionally, it has been found that the $a
u$MSM model may be favored over a related model incorporating only active neutrinos, known as the MSM. specifically, it has been discovered that the optimal range of axion masses for dark matter composition in the $a

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, surpassing the previous best-known estimate of $\alpha\leq 0.463$. This advancement allows for the development of a classical algorithm capable of approximating the output probabilities of $n$-qubit Clifford + T circuits $U$ within a specified inverse polynomial error margin, using a time complexity of $\mathrm{poly}(n,m)2^{\alpha m}$. Furthermore, the investigation yields optimized bounds for the stabilizer rank of symmetric product states $|\psi\rangle^{\otimes m}$ and $|\phi\rangle^{\otimes m}\otimes|\psi\rangle^{\otimes m}$. In specific instances, the algorithm can classically simulate quantum circuits whose gate complexity is substantially higher than its bit complexity, demonstrating the promise of providing a classical alternative to quantum algorithms.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, namely when the quantum correction in the Ricci scalar is non-zero and when the quintessence field is complex. The initial scenario determines the value of $n$ and $q_0$ through energy density equality in two different complex field scenarios, while the second scenario, with the complex field, yields values of $n$, $q_0$, and $m^2$ via the same energy density equality process. Notably, the real part of $m^2$ is negative in all cases, while its absolute value increases with higher $n$ values.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low and medium resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a total of 6309 optical counterparts for two micron excess sources. 5066 of these sources have never been observed before by LAMOST, and the study focused on their basic features, including their stellar classification, luminosity, motion, and mass. It was discovered that a subgroup of these sources, primarily composed of late-type stars with trigonometric parallax measurements less than 50 parsecs, exhibit greater motion than the overall source population. Furthermore, the study found that late-type stars with temperatures below 3000K and masses between 0.15 and 0.25 solar masses are more active than those with temperatures between 3000K and 4000K and similar masses. Data from multiple observational datasets confirm that the LAMOST data are reliable. The study's findings are consistent with those of a previous study (Hou et al. 2018) and provide further evidence for a well-established relationship between a giant low-frequency fluctuation and the high movement of late-type stars with certain properties.

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As SRAM cells are sensitive to process variations, changing their access patterns can inadvertently introduce randomness. To address this, this study proposes TuRaN, a method for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays by reducing the supply voltage and modifying the refresh pattern. To optimize TuRaN's performance, an evaluation was conducted across three different access schemes: sequential, parallel, and a combination of both. The results indicate that the refresh patterns introducing moderate amounts of data corruption and considering the SRAM cell's mean bias yield the best results. To further improve efficiency, multiplexing circuits were implemented, demonstrating an enhancement in entropy yield and reduced hardware requirements. Evaluation of TuRaN demonstrated a substantial enhancement in bits per second and reduction in bits per hertz performance compared to existing SRAM-based TRNGs.

We design and simulate two molecular devices, one a single-component device and the other a multi-component device, both of which exhibit single-electron resistive switching properties. The fundamental mechanism behind this phenomenon is understood to be either single-electron tunneling or a change in the device's conductive state, and we find that the device's structure and components significantly impact its resistive switching properties. The simulation results reveal that a multi-component device with a fixed central molecule demonstrates stable single-electron resistive switching, whereas a device with a mobile central molecule exhibits unstable switching properties. Additionally, we examine the impact of external electric fields on the switching process and find that a specific field strength can restore the device's switching function even after it has been weakened by a previous strong field. These simulations provide valuable insights for designing efficient single-electron resistive switches at the molecular level.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a unifying framework for numerical evaluations of multi-loop Feynman integrals beyond conventional computational methods. By applying loop-tree duality, numerical results for scattering amplitudes can be calculated directly without relying on mathematical expressions for their coefficients. In this review, we will delve into the theoretical foundations of loop-tree duality, present a standard procedure for its implementation and provide numerical case studies as examples. Additionally, we will address potential challenges and obstacles associated with applying loop-tree duality to complex scenarios involving massless particles, multi-loop integrals with multiple distinct loops, and the evaluation of virtual corrections.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on Sturm-Liouville operators by renowned mathematicians. A related theory involving the CMV matrix already addressed this topic, yet our approach is unique as it focuses specifically on the mentioned quantum walks and also yields valuable properties of Green functions. These properties enable us to derive a precise formula for a positive-matrix-valued measure, ultimately allowing for a direct computation of the spectral measure in a particular model known as the two-phase model.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical behavior within a linearly coupled $q$-deformed optomechanical system. Composed of two deformed cavities connected by an optomechanical interface, this study reveals that $q$-deformation enhances the speed and magnitude of light slowdown, while also discovering new optical transitions. Analysis shows that light can remain completely transparent through the $q$-deformed optomechanical system at specific resonance frequencies, and that $q$-deformation can amplify the optical system's sensitivity. Furthermore, research finds that certain $q$-deformation values can increase the light slowdown within the system by as much as five times, and that the system can exhibit nearly total transmission of light across a broad spectral range.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections in an internal plane related to R-symmetry, specifically focusing on I_R. This investigation led to a discovery, namely that I_R reflects the structure of the negative scissors state, reversing its orientation. Furthermore, I derived relationships between I_R and electric dipole transitions, which relate to R-symmetry, and found that these transitions can be interpreted as K-rotational scissors states, with or without R-parity.

The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts, and are also distinct from other covalent materials. By growing a monolayer of LaAlO3 on a stable SrO terminated surface of SrTiO3 (STO), and then patterning the resulting nanostructures using electron beam lithography and oxidation, we have explored the physical properties of these samples and compared them to those of standalone LaAlO3. Our findings reveal that the materials exhibit strong non-equilibrium orbital ordering at interfaces, and coexist with magnetic ordering brought about by electron orbital ordering. Our research indicates that these materials exhibit non-equilibrium internal states, and our data suggest that these materials can be viewed as a unique combination of an AT type Mott insulator and a d-band metal. Additionally, our research has shown that the materials exhibit unique fluctuations of spin and orbit, and these materials may display unique spontaneous symmetry breaking. Our research has great potential to explore the materials at the interface of quantum mechanics and general physics, and may provide valuable insights into the materials at the interface of quantum mechanics and general physics, and the resulting physical properties.

The occurrence of diffusion can be seen across various natural phenomena, and this widespread application is attributed to the broad implications of the central limit theorem. In the past, scientists discovered that individual, normally distributed components could give rise to non-Gaussian diffusion through a combination of these components. Moreover, non-normal independent components can form non-normal dependent diffusion processes. In this research, the authors explored a less-studied scenario, wherein non-normal independent components, coexisting with a common normal component, yielded distinctive, anomalous diffusion. To illustrate this phenomenon, the authors drew upon experiments involving laser-cooled atoms in dissipative optical lattices. By simulating these experiments using a combination of normal and non-normal components, the authors demonstrated the emergence of unique diffusion processes, characterized by dynamics diverging from standard diffusion behavior. Furthermore, the authors analyzed and discussed the resulting diffusion processes in this context.

This study investigates the effects of information dissemination on cryptocurrency price movements, focusing on the role of trading connections between different digital currencies. By employing a nonlinear time series model that can capture complex relationships, researchers model the price dynamics of specific cryptocurrencies (nodes) based on the interactions with other cryptocurrencies (pairs and groups). The results of their analysis reveal the existence of significant links between digital currencies, with evidence showing that trading connections play a significant role in price movement. Specifically, the study finds that higher-order trading interactions among top-20 cryptocurrencies are highly significant, with evidence showing that trading bundles have a more profound impact on price changes compared to individual trading connections. Furthermore, researchers demonstrate that their proposed model outperforms linear models in terms of explainability and long-term price prediction accuracy, with their novel approach providing new insights into digital currency price dynamics.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial process influencing the atmosphere's cloud formation capabilities. In particular, the reaction of sulphuric acid with water is a key mechanism producing particles, and recent research has indicated that accounting for the vibrational energy of the molecules is essential in determining the reaction rates. In the study presented here, the potential of mean force between sulphuric acid and water molecules has been calculated using ab-initio molecular dynamics, and the results have revealed a significant positive contribution from the zero-point energy. Furthermore, the analysis has suggested a lower threshold for the hydrogen-bonded dimer, and the results have indicated that the enthalpy of dimerization obtained from the potential energy profile is lower than the experimental value by approximately 0.4 kJ/mol. However, when the zero-point energy contribution is considered, the discrepancy with the experimental enthalpy of dimerization is reduced to 0.2 kJ/mol.

We introduce CPPE, a novel method for compactifying high-dimensional data sets, specifically perception pairs, and develop PEPS, a metric space consisting of group equivariant operators. Our approach draws upon recent advancements in computer vision, leveraging efficient numerical methods to simplify the compactification of data sets. The proposed techniques are further illustrated through experiments within the DeepLab framework.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in space. However, this analogy doesn't hold perfectly in the thermal Hall effect, which can be observed in systems where microscopic particles move in a circle under the influence of an external magnetic field. By considering the relationship between temperature gradients and these particle movements, we've discovered that this thermal Hall effect doesn't fully respect the principles of gravity's analogy and, as a result, the relationships between conductivity, temperature gradients, and energy spectrum are more complex than initially thought. These findings apply broadly to various types of materials that exhibit thermal Hall effect.

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By combining theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we demonstrate that several widespread training heuristics, such as parameter and spectral regularization, as well as parameter initialization techniques, serve to control geometric complexity.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing. The key obstacle has been effectively training models to match the level of human grading. The primary cost associated with automated essay grading research involves labor costs, as it requires collecting a large dataset with annotations. Once obtained, these datasets can be used to train models in automated grading. In this study, we explored enhancing the size of an existing dataset through cross-domain data augmentation, which significantly improved the accuracy of the models. The findings reveal that using transfer learning with BERT achieves the best results, with a high F1 score of 0.895 when applying the BERT-based model to test data. Additionally, we discovered that using a combination of BERT and Transformer-LSTM models leads to superior performance compared to using BERT and Transformer models alone.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from such marginal independence models, with a specific focus on models for random graphs and matroids' independent set polytopes. We also explore numerical methods for parameter estimation through both Euclidean distance and maximum likelihood techniques and establish a database for small model examples.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To effectively allocate these opportunities, the government must decide which candidates to admit, taking into account the candidates' potential to benefit from the opportunity and the positive impact they can have on their surroundings. To make informed decisions, the government needs a clear understanding of the opportunities' effects on the social hierarchy. To achieve this, a theoretical model is developed and analyzed using concepts from the study of interdependent decision-making and social networks. The government's optimal strategy is identified, and its performance is compared to a policy of admitting candidates based on their potential to benefit, a rule that simplifies the decision-making process and is easily measurable in real-world scenarios.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which reveal that Delegated RingCT can process around 100 transactions per second while utilizing a global address book containing millions of stealth addresses.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons simultaneously produced in high-energy collisions between protons.  These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's data set that contains 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of information.  Separate searches for individual combinations of bosons, including W boson variations, have been done using several patterns of final particle arrangements.  Together, the signals for these processes indicate a cross-section of boson creation that is slightly larger than that predicted by the standard model, occurring 5.7 (expected to be 5.9) standard deviations above background noise.  Specifically, signals for individual W boson variations have a significance of around 3.3 to 3.4 standard deviations and the measured rates of boson creation are also recorded.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. This research paper addresses this issue by presenting a new, open-access UD Hebrew treebank. This corpus, created by sampling various topics from Hebrew Wikipedia, provides a much-needed upgrade to NLP's understanding of contemporary Hebrew. The project evaluates its own annotations and those of the existing HTB using both manual and automated methods. Results show the new corpus significantly improves Hebrew parsing accuracy when compared to the old HTB. Due to its extensive annotations, the new corpus enables state-of-the-art UDPipe models to achieve unprecedented results. Ultimately, the project hopes this new corpus will accelerate and diversify Hebrew NLP.

We maintain a fixed $p$ in the interval $1 \leq p < \infty$. Consider the $\ell_p$ space equipped with the standard norm and let $\mathcal{M}$ be a given measurable subset of $\ell_p$. Assume that $\mathcal{M}$ satisfies a certain lower-dimensional growth condition known as incompressibility. Given an $\varepsilon$-isometry $T$ from $\mathcal{M}$ to $\ell_p$, we show that it can be embedded into a smaller, yet comparable, dimensionally reduced space $\mathcal{Q} \subset \ell_p$ such that $T$ remains $\varepsilon$-isometric when restricted to $\mathcal{M}$. Specifically, the maximum dimension of $\mathcal{Q}$ is boundedly proportional to $\varepsilon^{-p}$ and an instance of this result is realized for incompressible subsets of $\ell_p$ with an application of an $\varepsilon$-isometry from $\ell_p$ to $\ell_q$ for $q < p$.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This limitation hampers cooperative learning, since adjusting an existing model to incorporate new knowledge often compromises performance on earlier tasks. To address this issue, our study focused on developing a method to enable cooperative learning between researchers and engineers, allowing them to combine tasks and develop versatile, efficient models. We present a solution called Task2Vector (T2V), an innovative technique where researchers and engineers assign a unique vector to each problem, enabling the re-creation of previous models when training on new tasks. Through mathematical analysis and computer simulations, we demonstrate T2V's effectiveness and verify its potential to facilitate collaborative research.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs.

An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded safety area for linear systems impacted by bounded disturbances. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures system safety with fewer and less extreme adjustments to control inputs. Furthermore, we propose a specific variant of SL-MPSF that retains scalability and significantly decreases online processing requirements, which is the major drawback of traditional MPSF designs. The benefits of our safety filter design over state-of-the-art MPSF designs are demonstrated through numerical examples.

A critical flaw exists in quantum key distribution networks, specifically when using vacuum and weak coherent signal states, as they can be easily hijacked. However, researchers recently developed a more robust method by replacing random phase with partial random phase, which significantly enhances security. Nevertheless, a novel attack has been discovered which exploits the inherent flaws in partial random phase distribution, allowing a sophisticated hacker to guess key information. Our analysis reveals that even with the most secure settings, the proposed attack can still succeed and allows us to calculate the final key information generated within a specific distance from the initial sender.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in context impacts the shift from pretraining to fine-tuning. Our research explores the influence of the pretraining corpus on in-context learning by modifying the pretraining dataset of BERT and RoBERTa to include out-of-distribution data. Our findings show that in-context learning is highly dependent on the pretraining corpus, with a significant increase in test accuracy when the pretraining and test datasets share the same label spaces but originate from different sources. However, our results also indicate that in-context learning can lead to adverse effects, such as fine-tuning instability and a decrease in task accuracy in cases where the pre and fine-tuning datasets do not overlap.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of these formations disintegrates. To investigate the long-term effects of this process, we conducted 30 magnetohydrodynamic simulations of kiloparsec-scale, kiloparsec cold clouds within a galaxy cluster environment, considering various parameters such as magnetic strength and thermal equilibrium. The results show that the long-term mass growth rate of these clouds is significantly influenced by their initial conditions and surrounding magnetic fields, with an optimal balance between magnetic and thermal processes leading to substantial mass increase. On the other hand, situations with either highly dominant magnetic fields or near-equal magnetic and thermal processes lead to minimal mass growth, while extremely conductive or highly unstable situations result in net mass loss. Furthermore, it is revealed that the dissolution of kiloparsec-scale clouds leads to the creation of smaller, darker, high-density clumps that continue to exist for an extended period, a discovery that may hold implications for the long-standing problem of missing galactic luminosity at low masses.

The examination of $C\!P$ violation in beauty- and charm-hadron decays serves as a crucial test of the Standard Model's predictions, also acting as a sensitive indicator to uncover physical phenomena not accounted for within the SM. The presentation focuses on the latest $C\!P$ violation measurements in beauty- and charm-hadrons, in addition to recent studies concerning the determination of the angle $\beta_s$ and a comparison with theory predictions. This research is complemented by initial findings on the angle $\beta_c$ that governs $C\!P$ violation in charm hadrons. The presentations from the 2019 and 2021 CPV workshops are drawn upon to provide an overview of ongoing and planned studies at beauty and charm facilities, including those at CERN, Fermilab, and KEK. The material presented within this chapter does not encompass any new or proprietary data but rather a compilation of existing results along with future projections.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have unique polarization properties and their counterparts in bosonic string theory are significantly weaker. A remarkable relationship exists among these amplitudes, where one is proportional to the others. Calculations of their ratios confirm a long-standing theory prediction made by Gross in 1988. Additionally, the total count of newly calculated high-energy amplitudes in superstring theory is consistent with those from recently discovered fermion interactions in string theory.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data generated by a large number of cell towers, especially in rapidly growing urban areas, we need to develop specialized software. This paper focuses on creating efficient algorithms for managing urban cell tower data and developing strategies for optimizing urban cell tower deployments. We introduce a set of core network management procedures that enable self-organizing and sustainable 5G cellular networks. Specifically, we develop a decision-making system that enables urban cell tower management through a process called differential map formation. We also leverage the concepts of imitation game theory to create efficient algorithms for detecting and resolving conflicts between adjacent cell towers and developing sustainable 5G network planning strategies.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. Transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. We propose a unit clustering approach that utilizes a Markov cluster algorithm, analyzing the spectrogram trajectory instead of traditional Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients. Following the analysis, we employ a hidden Markov model to generate units and combine them with diphone-based synthesis via unit-by-unit synthesis, resulting in noticeable improvements over existing zero-speech synthesis methods.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion planning through multi-stage decision making has proven effective, yet its computational demands can be excessive and unaffordable. To tackle this issue, researchers have applied data-driven McCormick envelope relaxations to practical problems with positive results. This method involves using initial problem solutions to establish correlations between decision variables and their bounds, which are then reflected in relaxations of the associated optimization problems. This approach has been shown to yield efficient relaxations and lead to near-optimal planning results on simpler robots. However, the extension of this technique to more complex robots has not been successful thus far. In a recent study, researchers addressed this limitation by designing a multi-stage optimization framework that integrates coupled convex programming with data-driven relaxations. This novel method makes two key contributions. Firstly, it uses observed values of decision variables to create more accurate bounds for their relationships. Secondly, it applies these bounds to relax the associated optimization problems in a manner that is beneficial for solution improvement. This technique has been successfully applied to a 3D climbing robot and produced significantly better results, with solution quality increasing proportionally to the number of robot stages.

We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource metric.
This approach led to the discovery that the metric is not only necessary, but also sufficient, for one-shot resource conversion in various resource theories, effectively rendering more restrictive protocols unnecessary.
By employing this metric, we were able to precisely calculate the probability of achieving a desired transformation and thereby determined a crucial lower limit on the efficiency of probabilistic protocols.
Consequently, our results enabled a precise comparison between different resource metrics and their associated protocols.
Moreover, we introduced a method for quantifying the distance between quantum states based on achievable success probabilities in one-shot protocols.
This distance measure is not only simpler, but also more versatile than previously established options.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the averaging method helped to establish stability boundaries for two steady-state solutions, whereas vertical and horizontal excitations led to system resonances identified through multiple scale methods, with results validated using exact numerical integration techniques.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate that DR-DSGD outperforms DSGD and Regularized DSGD in non-robust scenarios, while also performing competitively in a robust setting.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues to utilize our research to determine non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field strengths and mass accumulation rates. The data show that strongly magnetized clouds produce fast-moving jets only when the protostar gains a relatively small amount of mass per year, typically no more than 10 to the minus 3 solar masses. However, this low-mass rate also means that less-strong magnetic fields are required to produce the high-velocity jets. For very high mass accumulation rates, the high-velocity jets appear initially, but quickly weaken and then suddenly disappear around a certain threshold rate, after which they are entirely replaced by low-velocity jets that require no magnetic field to wind down. The high-velocity jets can explain only a small portion of the low-velocity flow observed in protostars, indicating that other factors must also contribute significantly.

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced tumor growth therapy and chemical reaction control, through a novel analysis that leverages the system's intrinsic characteristics and limitations. A specific cost function is employed to evaluate performance under real-world constraints, such as system parameter boundaries, and the system's behavior is analyzed under these constraints using the system's relative degree and entropy measure. A quantitative assessment of performance degradation due to performance losses is developed, and an optimal performance efficiency metric is defined, which maximizes system performance without exceeding the specified bounds, thereby ensuring the system remains within operational limits. This framework is further illustrated through the application to balanced tumor therapy systems.

This research investigates the impact of solar pressure on the orbits of artificial satellites around Earth, specifically exploring how their perturbations interact with commensurabilities that produce quasi-periodic variations. By identifying and analyzing the boundaries defining these resonance zones, it's possible to determine the influence of solar pressure on orbital stability. That assessment is further refined to account for Equatorial Bulge effects in order to provide even more accurate predictions. To validate its models, the research team conducted numerical simulations comparing analytical and numerical estimates for various orbital parameters, demonstrating the utility of these estimates in predicting the effects of solar pressure.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models derived from first-principle calculations, specifically considering the dipole approximation and ultrastrong-coupling regimes. We propose a method for ensuring the models' gauge invariance, allowing for the construction of physically valid models despite lattice irregularity and coupling strength. We apply our approach to a simple hydrogen molecule and a more complex copper phthalocyanine-Co atom, achieving accurate results that align with both experimental data and quantum mechanical simulations. Our methodology provides a foundation for accurately modeling the behavior of strong light-matter couplings in large, complex systems.

In a problem focused on category-level perception, we consider using sensor data to identify and understand objects within specific categories despite variations within those categories. An active shape model, where pre-defined CAD models of various objects are used as a reference, is employed to determine the 3D pose and shape of an object. Our work begins by identifying an optimal solution for combining 2D and 3D sensor data, using sensor constraints and category-specific variations as key factors. Additionally, we develop robust methods to handle potential issues, including outliers and discrepancies in sensor data quality. The effectiveness of our methods is tested on the PASCAL3D+ dataset, with impressive results showing accurate object localization and classification. Our code is available for review at https://github.com/stevenlizi/P3DES.
